unit.title: Undertake fabrication, forming, bending and shaping

summary: This unit teaches you to turn sheet, plate, bar, sections and pipe into finished parts: planning from the drawing, cutting blanks, and bending, folding, rolling and hand forming them to shape. You will learn to use fabrication machines safely, work out blank sizes and bend allowances, allow for springback, roll cylinders to size, assemble and tack parts square, and check, finish and report on your work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It covers the shaping side of fabrication: **cutting** sheet, plate and sections to size, **bending and folding** them, **rolling** plate into cylinders and bar into rings, **forming** sheet by hand, and **assembling** the parts so the finished job matches the drawing.

Welding joins the parts, but fabrication makes them. In Jamaica fabricators make hurricane shutters, roof flashings and gutters, range hoods and ducting for kitchens and jerk centres, water-tank stands, chimneys and exhaust stacks, handrails, gates, trailer bodies, storage tanks and machine guards. Each starts as flat sheet, plate or straight lengths, and each must come out square, to size and safe to handle.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You will use the guillotine, snips, box and pan folder, press brake, bending rolls, bar bender, pipe bender and hand forming tools on mild steel and galvanised sheet, flat bar and pipe.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Read the drawing, make a cutting list, work out blank sizes and allowances, plan the order of work, and check the materials and machines.
Use each machine only as trained, keep hands clear of blades, nips and tools, isolate before adjusting or clearing, handle sheet and long lengths safely.
Cut blanks square and to size with the right machine or hand tool, deburr them, mark bend lines from a datum, and notch corners.
Fold sheet on the box and pan folder and press brake, bend bar and pipe, allow for springback, and form sheet by hand.
Work out the plate length for a cylinder, pre-bend the ends, roll to shape and check it with a template.
Set parts in a jig or against stops, tack them, and check that frames are square and flat before full welding.
Measure against the drawing and its tolerances, finish edges and surfaces, keep the area tidy, and report faults and parts that are out of tolerance.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, materials, cutting, bending, allowances, rolling, pipe bending, hot and cold forming, hand forming, assembly and checking.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words and simple sums: stake, planishing hammer, blank, work hardening, flange, nibbler, former, the neutral axis radius) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: marking out, notching and folding a sheet metal tray with hemmed edges; and working out, rolling and tacking a small cylinder, then cold-bending a flat bar to 90°.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to the theory papers and practise the two sums in this kit until they are automatic: the bend allowance and the length of plate for a cylinder.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Read the **whole** drawing before you cut anything: the title block, the scale, the material and its thickness, every view, the sizes, the tolerances and the notes.
Check it is the **latest issue**: look at the revision letter or date.
Find the **datum**: the edge, face or line the sizes are measured from.
Ask your supervisor or instructor about anything that is not clear. Never guess a size.

head: Section
Shape
How its size is written (example)
Typical uses
rows: Rectangular or square hollow section (RHS or SHS)
Outside diameter × wall, or nominal bore
Sheet (thin, up to about 3 mm) for trays, ducting and covers; plate (thicker) for bases, brackets and tanks

blocks.note: Corrugated roofing sheet is called **zinc** in Jamaica, because it is galvanised (zinc-coated) steel. Galvanised sheet is used for flashings, gutters and ducting. Wear gloves: its edges are very sharp, and in the sun it gets hot enough to burn.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **cutting list** lists every part of the job, with its material, size and the number needed. It lets you check the stock, cut everything in one go and waste less. A flat piece cut to size and shape before it is folded or rolled is called a **blank**.

A **tolerance** is how far a size may be from the drawing and still be acceptable. A size of 300 ± 1 mm may measure anything from 299 to 301 mm. Measure carefully, with tools in good order, and remember that every cut, bend and weld can move a size.

flow: Read the drawing and make the cutting list
Check the material: right type, thickness and size, not damaged or badly rusted
Do a risk assessment: sharp edges, heavy lifts, machine nips, noise, hot work
Cut the blanks and parts, and deburr them
Mark the bend lines and holes from the datum
Notch corners and drill or punch holes while the part is flat
Bend, fold, roll or form
Assemble in a jig or against stops, and tack
Check the sizes, squareness and flatness
Weld or join, check again, finish, and record the results

blocks.note: Plan the bending order before you start. A flange bent too early can stop the part fitting into the folder or press brake for the next bend.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working safely with sheet, plate and machines

blocks.p: Fabrication machines are powerful enough to crush, cut or amputate in a moment, and sheet edges cut as deeply as a knife. Use a machine only when you have been **trained** on it and your instructor has **allowed** you to use it.

head: Machine or task
Main danger
How you control it
rows: Fingers crushed by the hold-downs or cut off by the blade; reaching behind the machine
**One person only** works the pedal, when everyone's hands are clear
Never reach behind while it can run
Hands crushed between the punch and the die; the sheet whipping up as it bends
Hold the sheet by its outer edges, hands well clear of the tools
Guards, light curtains or two-hand controls in use
Stand clear of the rising sheet
Fingers trapped under the clamp bar or by the swinging leaf
Nobody else reaches in while you work it
Hands, gloves, sleeves or rags drawn into the **nip** between the rolls
Keep hands and loose clothing away from the nip
Feed from the side, not by pushing at the nip
Fingers caught between the work and the former; a bar slipping
Fingers clear of the former and guide
Blade contact; a disc bursting; sparks
Deep cuts from edges; back injuries; long lengths swinging into people
Two or more people for long or heavy pieces, lifting together on a signal
Sheet carried on edge, not flat over the head

blocks.p: Before you change tooling, adjust a guard, clear a jam or reach into a machine, **switch it off and isolate it**: turn off the isolator and lock it off (or remove the plug) so no one can start it while your hands are inside. The red **emergency stop** button stops a machine at once in an emergency, but it is not a safe way to work inside a machine.

flow: Stop the machine
Switch off and lock off the isolator, or unplug it and keep the plug with you
Try the start button to prove it will not run
Do the work
Remove your tools, refit the guards, then remove the lock and test

ul: Leather or cut-resistant **gloves** for handling sheet, blanks and offcuts; remove them near rotating parts where a glove could be caught (for example at the nip of the rolls), as your instructor says.
**Safety glasses** at all times; a face shield for grinding and abrasive cutting.
**Safety boots** against dropped plate and offcuts.
**Ear protection** for hammering, guillotining heavy sheet and grinding.
Close-fitting overalls, sleeves buttoned, no loose cuffs, rings or chains near machines.

blocks.note: Report any machine fault straight away: a grinding noise, slipping, a guard that will not stay in place, a pedal that sticks. Stop, isolate the machine, and tell your instructor before anyone uses it again.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: How metal behaves when it is formed

blocks.p: Bend a strip of steel a little and let go: it springs back straight. That is **elastic** bending. Bend it further and it stays bent: the metal has been **plastically** deformed. Fabrication uses plastic bending, but part of every bend is still elastic, so when the force is taken off, the bend opens up slightly. This is **springback**.

head: More springback
Less springback
rows: Harder, higher-strength metals: high-tensile steel, spring steel, stainless steel
Thinner material bent to the same radius
Metal that has been work hardened
Metal pressed fully into the die (bottoming)

blocks.p: Fabricators allow for springback by **over-bending**: bending a little past the angle needed, so the part springs back to it. The amount comes from experience, the machine maker's tables, or a **test bend** on an offcut of the same material. Check every bend with a square, protractor or angle gauge before moving on.

When metal is bent, the **outside** of the bend is stretched and gets thinner, and the **inside** is squeezed and gets thicker. Somewhere in between is a layer that is neither stretched nor squeezed: the **neutral axis**. Its length does not change, so it is the line used to work out how much metal a bend uses. For workshop sums we take it as the **middle of the thickness**. (In tight bends in thin sheet it moves a little towards the inside, so check accurate work with a test bend.)

ul: Every metal has a smallest **inside bend radius** it can take without cracking on the outside. Harder metals and thicker plate need a bigger radius. The drawing or the maker's table gives it.

Rolled sheet and plate have a **grain**: the direction they were rolled in. Bends made **across the grain** are less likely to crack than bends made along it. Plan your blanks so the important bends run across the grain.
Do not mark bend lines with a deep **scribed** line or centre-punch marks on the outside of the bend: the stretching opens them into cracks. Use a pencil or fine marker there.
Remove burrs and nicks from the edges before bending: cracks start at them.

blocks.p: Bending, hammering and rolling cold metal make it harder, stiffer and more brittle: **work hardening**. Keep working it and it cracks. **Annealing** softens it again so it can be worked further:

head: Metal
How it is annealed (follow your instructor)
rows: Heated to a red heat and left to cool slowly
Heated to a dull red; it can then be cooled in water or in air, and is soft either way
Heated to a much lower temperature, judged with a soap or marker test your instructor will show you, then cooled; it gives no glow to warn you

head: Point
Cold forming
Hot forming
rows: Shaping at room temperature with machines or hand tools
Shaping after heating, usually to a bright red, with a torch or furnace
Thick bar and heavy sections can be bent
Work hardening; cracking on tight bends
Folding sheet, rolling plate, bending light flat bar and pipe, repeat work
Bending thick bar into hooks and scrolls, heavy sections, one-off bends

head: Tool or machine
Best for
Points to know
rows: Straight cuts in sheet and thin plate
Its rated capacity is for **mild steel**; harder metals such as stainless steel must be thinner (often about two-thirds of the mild steel figure)
Set the back gauge and check it with a rule
Never cut round bar, wire or anything it is not made for
Straight cuts and gentle curves in thin sheet
Aviation snips often have **yellow** handles for straight cuts
Curves and corners in thin sheet
Left-cut (often **red** handles) cut curves to the left; right-cut (often **green**) to the right
Straight and curved cuts in thicker sheet
Lever action; keep fingers clear of the blades
Shapes and curves in sheet, cut by punching out many small bites
Leaves small crescent-shaped waste: wear glasses
Right blade for the material; guard down close to the work; work clamped
Sparks and heat; disc rated for the speed; leaves a burr
Covered in the thermal cutting unit

ul: Measure every line from **one datum edge**. Measuring each line from the last one adds up small errors.
Mark cut lines with a scriber or fine marker; mark bend lines with a pencil or fine marker on the face that will be the outside of the bend.
Use an engineer's square for square lines and a steel rule or tape for lengths; check the blank is square by measuring its diagonals.
Allow for the saw cut (the kerf) when marking several parts from one length.

blocks.p: Every cut edge has a **burr**: a thin, sharp lip of metal. Remove it with a file, a deburring tool or a flap disc before the part is folded or handled. Burrs cut hands, stop parts fitting, spoil folds and start cracks.

Where two bend lines cross at a corner, the metal has nowhere to go. **Notch** the corner (cut a square or V out of it) so the sides fold up without bulging or overlapping. A small relief cut or hole at the inside corner, where the two bend lines meet, stops the sheet tearing as it folds.

sections.title: Bending and folding sheet, bar and pipe

blocks.h: Working out a blank: the bend allowance

blocks.p: The **bend allowance** is the length of metal used up in the curved part of a bend, measured along the neutral axis. For a 90° bend:

ul: Neutral axis radius = inside radius + half the thickness
Bend allowance = 2 × π × neutral axis radius × (angle ÷ 360); for 90°, that is the neutral axis radius × 1.571
Blank length = the straight (flat) lengths + the bend allowance

head: Worked example: an L-bracket in 2 mm sheet
Working
rows: Outside leg sizes 50 mm and 30 mm; inside bend radius 4 mm; 90° bend
Each outside leg less the inside radius and the thickness: 50 − 6 = 44 mm and 30 − 6 = 24 mm

blocks.note: For thin sheet folded with a sharp bend (an inside radius close to zero), the allowance is small, and simple trays are often marked out as base plus sides. For accurate work, make a test bend on an offcut and measure it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Edge
What it is
Allowance and use
rows: An edge bent up, often at 90°
Stiffens a panel or gives a face to fix to
The edge folded right back flat on itself
Stiffens the edge and removes the sharp edge; allow the width of the hem
The edge rolled round a wire
Stiffens and makes safe a curved or long edge; a common allowance is about **2.5 × the wire diameter**
Two folded edges hooked together and locked down with a hand groover
Joins sheets; a common allowance is three times the seam width, split between the two sheets

blocks.p: A **box and pan folder** (pan brake) clamps the sheet under a clamp bar made of separate **fingers**, then a folding leaf swings up to fold it. Because the fingers can be taken out or moved, the clamp can be made to fit **between** sides already folded, so the last two sides of a box or tray can be folded.

head: Worked example: tray blank
Working
rows: Base 200 × 120 mm, sides 30 mm high, sharp folds in 1 mm sheet
A 30 × 30 mm square cut from each corner
If two sides have a hem, add the hem width to those sides

flow: Work out the blank size from the drawing; cut it square on the guillotine and deburr it
Mark the bend lines from one datum edge; mark and cut the corner notches with snips, with a small relief at each inside corner
Fold any hems first, while the sheet is still flat
Set the folder's fingers to the base length, line the bend line up with the clamping edge, and clamp
Fold the first two opposite sides, just past 90° to allow for springback
Reset the fingers so the clamp fits between the folded sides, then fold the other two sides
Check the sides with a square and the sizes with a rule; finish the corners as the drawing shows

blocks.p: A **press brake** forms a bend by pressing the sheet or plate into a **V-shaped die** with a **punch**. A back gauge sets where the bend falls. In **air bending** the punch pushes the sheet only part way into the die, and the depth sets the angle; in **bottoming** the sheet is pressed fully into the die, which reduces springback. Hold the sheet by its outer edges, keep your hands clear of the tools, and stand clear as the sheet rises.

ul: Mark the bend line; set the bar in the bender or vice with the line at the edge of the former or jaws.
Bend steadily, a little past the angle to allow for springback; check with a square or protractor.
Thick bar may need heat (see the thermal cutting and heating unit), or a bigger machine; never force a bend the machine is not rated for.

flow: Check the drawing for the bend angle, the radius and where each bend starts
Choose a **former** and guide that match the pipe's **outside diameter**
Mark the start of the bend on the pipe, measured from the datum end
Turn a welded seam to the **side**, on the neutral axis, not the inside or outside of the bend
Line the mark up with the start of the former and bend slowly and steadily, a little past the angle for springback
Check the angle with a square or protractor

head: Pipe bending fault
Cause
Prevention
rows: Wrong size former or guide; no support for the wall
Former and guide matched to the outside diameter
Bending too fast or too tight; former too small
Steady bending; never tighter than the former is made for
Wrinkling on the inside of the bend
Radius too tight for the pipe; wall not supported
Larger radius; support the wall (mandrel or packing) as your instructor says
Radius too tight; seam on the outside; hard pipe
Correct radius; seam at the side

blocks.p: For hot bends, or very tight bends in thin-walled pipe, the pipe is packed tightly with **dry** sand and plugged at both ends to support the walls. The sand must be completely dry: water in it turns to steam and can blow a plug out with great force.

blocks.h: The length of plate for a cylinder

blocks.p: When plate is rolled, the outside stretches and the inside squeezes, just as in bending. The length of plate needed is the length of the **neutral axis**, at the middle of the thickness. So the sum uses the **mean diameter**:

ul: Mean diameter = outside diameter − thickness, or inside diameter + thickness
Length of plate = mean diameter × π (π is about 3.142)

head: Worked example: a cylinder 400 mm inside diameter in 5 mm plate
Working
rows: Using the outside diameter (410 mm) gives 1 288 mm: 16 mm too long, so the seam will not close properly

blocks.p: Most workshops use **three-roll bending rolls**: two rolls grip the plate and the third presses it into a curve as it passes through. Hand-cranked **slip rolls** do the same for thin sheet. A **section roller** has shaped rolls for rolling angle, flat bar and channel into rings.

flow: Work out the plate length from the mean diameter; cut the plate square, so the seam will line up, and deburr it
**Pre-bend both ends** on the press brake or in the rolls: the rolls cannot curve the last part of each end, which would be left flat
Make a template to the right radius from thin sheet or card
Feed the plate in **square** to the rolls, with the rolls set parallel
Tighten the rolls a little at each pass and roll the plate back and forth, so the curve is made over several passes, never all at once
Keep hands, gloves and clothing clear of the nip; work the controls from the safe side
Check the curve often with the template
When the edges meet, check the gap and line them up with clamps; tack the seam
Check roundness by measuring the diameter in several places

head: Rolling fault
Likely cause
rows: Flat areas each side of the seam
One end tighter than the other (a cone shape)
Plate fed in at an angle, or rolls not parallel
Edges that do not meet, or overlap
Plate length worked out from the wrong diameter, or rolled too loose or too tight
Uneven passes; the plate not rolled evenly all along
Plate cut out of square, or edges not lined up before tacking

blocks.note: Rolls do not stop just because something is caught in them. If a glove, sleeve or rag is drawn towards the nip, hit the emergency stop at once, and never try to pull it out while the rolls can turn.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many shapes are still made by hand, with stakes, mallets and hammers, especially one-off jobs, repairs and curved work.

head: Tool
What it is
Used for
rows: Shaped steel blocks held in the bench or in a stake holder: hatchet, half-moon, funnel, bick iron, round-head and others
Forming sheet over: folding, curving, wiring edges and shaping round work
Forming thin sheet without denting or stretching it
A mallet with a rounded, egg-shaped head
Hollowing sheet into a sandbag or a hollowed block
A hammer with smooth, polished, slightly domed faces
Smoothing out the marks of hollowing and raising
A hammer with long, rounded faces
Bending and folding a sheet edge by hand
A steel tool with a groove in its end
Closing and locking down a grooved seam with a hammer
A leather bag of sand, or a wooden block with shallow hollows

head: Method
How it is done
What happens to the metal
rows: The sheet is hammered from the inside into a sandbag or hollow block with a bossing mallet, working in circles from the outside edge towards the centre
It stretches and gets **thinner**, forming a shallow dish
The sheet is hammered from the outside over a stake, working round in rings from the base outwards
It is squeezed in and stays about the same thickness or gets a little thicker; deeper shapes such as bowls
The work is held on a polished stake that matches its shape and struck with light, even, overlapping blows of a planishing hammer
The bumps are smoothed out and the surface is lightly hardened
The edge is turned round a wire with a mallet on a hatchet stake (or in a wiring machine) and closed tightly
The edge is bent over a hatchet stake or the bench edge with a mallet, or with a hand seamer

ul: Strike with the **flat** of the mallet or hammer face, with light, even blows. Heavy blows stretch and dent thin sheet.
Hand-formed sheet **work hardens**. If it becomes springy or starts to crack at the edge, **anneal** it before going on.
Wear ear protection: hammering sheet is very loud.

blocks.note: The tool face and the stake must be clean and smooth. Every dent or speck of grit on them is printed into the work.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **jig** holds the parts in their right places so each one is assembled the same way, square and to size. It may be a frame of stops and clamps on a welding table, or blocks bolted to a bench. Even for a single job, setting parts against stops on a flat table and clamping them is the fastest way to get them right.

flow: Check that every member is cut to length, with clean, square or mitred ends, and deburred
Lay the parts out on a flat welding table or level trestles, against stops or in a jig, and clamp them
Check the joints fit closely with even gaps
Tack one corner and check it with a square, then tack the others
Measure both **diagonals**: if they differ, push along the **longer** diagonal until they are equal
Check the frame lies **flat**: if a corner rocks or lifts, the frame is twisted; clamp it flat and correct it
Add more tacks, evenly on both sides of each joint
Weld in a balanced order (opposite corners in turn) with short runs, keeping the frame clamped
Check the diagonals and flatness again after welding and as it cools

blocks.note: Diagonals are the fastest test of square. A frame whose two diagonals are equal is square; the bigger the difference, the further out of square it is.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
Use it when
Points to know
rows: A strong, permanent joint is needed
You can reach only **one side** of the job, for example sheet on a box frame
Drill the hole size the rivet maker gives; choose a rivet for the total thickness
Strong joints in sheet and light plate where welding is not wanted
The parts must come apart again, or be adjusted
Self-tapping screws for sheet; washers under soft metal
Grooved seam locked with a hand groover

ul: Use measuring tools in good order: steel rule, tape, engineer's square, protractor, radius gauges, templates and a straight edge.
Measure overall sizes, hole and bend positions, bend angles, and the radius of rolled parts, and compare each with the drawing and its tolerance.
Check **squareness** (diagonals), **flatness** (straight edge), and **roundness** (diameters in several places).
Look over the whole part for burrs, sharp edges, dents, cracks at the bends and weld faults.
Write the results on the job card.

blocks.h: When a part is out of tolerance

blocks.p: Do not hide it or pass it on. **Mark** the part, **tell** your supervisor or instructor, and agree whether it can be **reworked** (for example re-bent or re-squared) or must be **made again**. Find out why it happened so it does not happen on the next one.

ul: Remove burrs and round off sharp edges and corners.
Grind welds flush only where the drawing asks; remove spatter.
Clean off oil, marker and loose scale so paint will stick.
Prime and paint as the drawing says. On galvanised work, touch up any welded or ground areas with a zinc-rich paint.

blocks.note: Sea air and humidity rust bare steel within days in most of Jamaica. Prime fabricated steel promptly, and store finished work under cover, off the ground.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Sort offcuts into the offcut rack and scrap into the scrap bins (steel, stainless and aluminium apart), off the floor.
Keep walkways and machine areas clear: offcuts on the floor are a slip and cut hazard.
Isolate and clean the machines after use; return tools to their places.
Report machine faults (noises, slipping, damaged guards), injuries and near misses, material faults and out-of-tolerance parts to your instructor or supervisor.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a fabrication drawing and make a cutting list.
I can name the common steel sections and say how their sizes are written.
I can use each machine only as trained, keep my hands clear, and isolate a machine before adjusting or clearing it.
I can handle sheet and long lengths safely.
I can explain springback, the neutral axis, work hardening, annealing and bending across the grain.
I can compare hot and cold forming and say when to use each.
I can choose a cutting method, mark out from a datum, deburr, and notch corners.
I can work out a bend allowance and a blank length.
I can fold a tray on a box and pan folder, with hems first and an allowance for springback.
I can bend flat bar and pipe, and name pipe bending faults and how to prevent them.
I can work out the plate length for a cylinder from its mean diameter, roll it, and check it.
I can name hand forming tools and describe hollowing, raising, planishing and wiring an edge.
I can assemble a frame square and flat, using diagonals and a flat table.
I can check a part against the drawing, finish it, and say what to do if it is out of tolerance.
I can keep the work area tidy and report faults.

terms: Angle
A steel section shaped like a capital L
Annealing
Heating and cooling metal to soften it after it has work hardened
Bend allowance
The length of metal used up in the curved part of a bend
Blank
A flat piece cut to size and shape before it is folded or rolled
Box and pan folder
A folding machine with removable fingers, for boxes and trays; also called a pan brake
Burr
The sharp lip of metal left on a cut edge
Channel
A steel section shaped like a capital U or C
Cutting list
A list of every part, with its material, size and number needed
Datum
The edge, face or line all sizes are measured from
Emergency stop
The large red button that stops a machine at once
Flange
An edge bent up, often at 90°, to stiffen it
Former
The shaped block that a pipe or bar is bent around
Grain
The direction in which sheet or plate was rolled
Hem
An edge folded back flat on itself; also called a safe edge
Hollowing
Hammering sheet into a hollow so it stretches into a dish; also called sinking
Jig
A device that holds parts in place so each is assembled the same
Mean diameter
The diameter at the middle of the plate thickness
Neutral axis
The layer in a bend that is neither stretched nor squeezed
Nibbler
A tool that cuts sheet by punching out many small bites
Notch
A piece cut out of a corner so the sides fold without overlapping
Planishing hammer
A hammer with smooth, polished faces for smoothing formed sheet
Press brake
A machine that bends sheet and plate with a punch and a die
Raising
Hammering sheet over a stake to form a deep shape
Section roller
A machine that rolls angle, flat bar and channel into rings
Springback
The bend opening up a little when the bending force is removed
Stake
A shaped steel block that sheet is formed over by hand
Tolerance
How far a size may be from the drawing and still be acceptable
Wired edge
An edge rolled round a wire to stiffen it
Work hardening
Metal becoming harder and more brittle as it is worked cold

c1.title: A range hood in Boston, Portland
c1.text: Shamar is making a galvanised sheet range hood for a jerk centre in Boston, Portland, on a box and pan folder. The lower part is an open tray of 0.8 mm sheet with a hem along two edges. On his first try the sheet tore at the inside corners where the bend lines crossed, and after folding, the sides sprang back to about 87°. He has folded two opposite sides and now finds the clamp bar too wide to fit between them.

c2.title: A bakery chimney in Christiana
c2.text: Petagaye is rolling a chimney section for a bakery in Christiana, Manchester. The drawing gives an inside diameter of 300 mm in 3 mm mild steel plate. On her first attempt the cylinder came out tighter at one end than the other. While feeding the plate, a classmate's glove was pulled towards the rolls.

c3.title: Shelf brackets in Lucea
c3.text: At a fabrication shop in Lucea, Hanover, Tevin is bending L-shaped shelf brackets from 2 mm mild steel on the press brake. The drawing gives outside leg sizes of 40 mm and 25 mm and an inside bend radius of 2 mm. Several brackets have cracked on the outside of the bend. He had marked each bend line with a deep scribed line, and the blanks were cut so that the bend runs along the rolling direction of the sheet.

c4.title: Church handrails in Black River
c4.text: Oshane is bending steel pipe for new handrails at a church in Black River, St Elizabeth, using a hydraulic pipe bender. On the first bend the pipe went oval at the bend, and on a tighter bend the inside of the pipe wrinkled.

c5.title: A gate frame in Annotto Bay
c5.text: A team at a shop in Annotto Bay, St Mary, is assembling a gate frame from 50 × 50 × 3 mm square hollow section. The drawing gives an outside width of 1 200 ± 2 mm. After tacking, the diagonals measure 2 690 mm and 2 684 mm, and one corner of the frame lifts off the flat welding table when the opposite corner is pressed down.

questions.q: What would have stopped Shamar's sheet tearing at the inside corners?
o: Folding all four sides up at the same time
Using a thicker sheet of galvanised steel
A small relief cut at each inside corner
Folding the sides more slowly and gently
questions.why: Where two bend lines cross, the metal has nowhere to go and tears. A small relief cut or hole where the lines meet lets each side fold freely.

questions.q: In what order should the hems and sides of the tray be folded?
o: The hems first, while the sheet is still flat
The sides first, then the hems inside the tray
The two short sides first, then the hems and long sides
Any order, as long as every fold reaches 90°
questions.why: A hem needs the sheet lying flat in the folder. Once the sides are up, the edge to be hemmed can no longer be clamped and folded properly.

questions.q: How should Shamar get the sides to finish at 90°?
o: Fold them to exactly 90° and hammer them square afterwards
Fold them slightly past 90° so they spring back to 90°
Heat each fold line with a torch so it cannot spring back
Fold them to 87° on purpose and accept the result
questions.why: Part of every bend is elastic and springs back when the leaf is lowered. Folding a little past 90°, judged by a test fold, leaves the side at 90°.

questions.q: The clamp bar is too wide to fit between the two folded sides. What should he do?
o: Unfold one side, fold the short sides, then refold it
Fold the last two sides by hand over the bench edge
Clamp on top of the folded sides and fold through them
Remove fingers until the clamp fits between the sides
questions.why: The box and pan folder's clamp is made of separate fingers so it can be set to fit between sides already folded. That is what lets the last two sides of a tray be folded.

questions.q: How long should Petagaye's plate be for the 300 mm inside diameter in 3 mm plate?
o: About 942 mm
About 952 mm
About 961 mm
About 909 mm
questions.why: Use the mean diameter: 300 + 3 = 303 mm, and 303 × 3.142 ≈ 952 mm. Using the inside diameter alone (942 mm) or the outside diameter (961 mm) gives the wrong length.

questions.q: What most likely made the cylinder tighter at one end than the other?
o: Plate fed in at an angle, or rolls not parallel
Ends of the plate not pre-bent before rolling
Plate length worked out from the inside diameter
Rolls tightened only a little at each pass
questions.why: If the plate goes in out of square, or one end of the top roll is set lower, one end is curved more than the other and the cylinder becomes a cone. Missing pre-bends leave flats, not a cone.

questions.q: The glove is being drawn towards the nip. What must be done first?
o: Pull the hand and glove out as fast as possible
Reverse the rolls by hand to free the glove
Hit the emergency stop at once
Shout for the instructor and wait for help
questions.why: Rolls keep turning until they are stopped, and pulling against them can drag the hand in further. The emergency stop halts the machine at once; the hand is freed only when the rolls cannot move.

questions.q: When the edges meet, there is a 3 mm step between them along part of the seam. What should Petagaye do before tacking?
o: Tack it as it is and grind the step off later
Fill the step with extra weld when it is fully welded
Line the edges up with clamps, then tack the seam
Roll the whole cylinder tighter until the step closes
questions.why: A stepped seam makes a weak, ugly joint and an out-of-round cylinder. Clamping the edges level before tacking holds them in line for welding.

questions.q: Which change would most help stop Tevin's brackets cracking?
o: Bend them faster so the metal has less time to crack
Cut the blanks so the bend runs across the grain
Use a smaller inside radius so the bend is sharper
Mark the bend lines with deeper scribed lines
questions.why: Bends along the rolling direction crack more easily on the outside. Turning the blanks so the bends run across the grain, and using a pencil line, stops the cracking.

questions.q: Why did the deep scribed lines make the cracking worse?
o: The groove opens into a crack as the outside stretches
The scribing hardens the sheet all the way through it
The press brake punch catches on the scribed line
The scribed line shows the wrong position for the bend
questions.why: The outside of a bend is stretched, and a deep scratch there acts as the start of a crack. Bend lines are marked with a pencil or fine marker.

questions.q: Taking the neutral axis at mid-thickness, what is the blank length for Tevin's bracket?
o: About 65.0 mm
About 60.1 mm
About 57.0 mm
About 61.7 mm
questions.why: Straight lengths: 40 − (2 + 2) = 36 mm and 25 − 4 = 21 mm. Neutral radius 2 + 1 = 3 mm, so the bend allowance is 3 × 1.571 = 4.7 mm. Total: 36 + 21 + 4.7 = 61.7 mm.

questions.q: What most likely made the pipe go oval at the bend?
o: The pipe was bent a little past the angle it needed
The bend was made too slowly and steadily
The former and guide did not match the pipe's size
The start of the bend was marked on the pipe
questions.why: A former and guide that do not fit the pipe's outside diameter leave the wall unsupported, so it flattens. Always match them to the pipe.

questions.q: What should Oshane do to stop the inside of the tighter bend wrinkling?
o: Use a larger radius, or support the pipe wall
Bend it faster so the wall has no time to fold
Turn the welded seam to the inside of the bend
Cool the pipe with water while he bends it
questions.why: Wrinkles form when the inside of a bend is squeezed more than the wall can take. A larger radius, or supporting the wall as the instructor directs, prevents them.

questions.q: The diagonals measure 2 690 mm and 2 684 mm. What should the team do?
o: Push along the shorter diagonal so that it gets longer
Push along the longer diagonal until they are equal
Leave it, since 6 mm is small on a frame this size
Cut 6 mm off the longest side and re-tack it
questions.why: Equal diagonals mean the frame is square. Pushing the corners on the longer diagonal towards each other shortens it and lengthens the other until they match.

questions.q: What does it mean when one corner lifts as the opposite corner is pressed down?
o: The frame is twisted and must be clamped flat
The welding table needs to be levelled first
The diagonals must be unequal by the same amount
The tacks are too strong and must be ground off
questions.why: A frame that rocks on a flat table is twisted (in wind). It is clamped flat to the table and corrected before more tacks or welding lock the twist in.

questions.q: After welding, the frame measures 1 197 mm wide. What should the team do?
o: Pass it on, since 3 mm is close enough on a garden gate
Mark it, tell the supervisor, and agree how to fix it
Stretch it with a jack until the tape reads 1 200 mm
Change the size on the drawing to read 1 197 mm
questions.why: 1 200 ± 2 mm allows 1 198 to 1 202 mm, so 1 197 mm is out of tolerance. The part is marked and reported, and rework or remaking is agreed; it is never hidden.

questions.q: Before the gate is painted for a house near the sea, what should be done?
o: Paint straight over the spatter and mill scale
Leave it unpainted for a week to weather first
Wash it down with seawater to remove the oil
Deburr and clean it, then prime it promptly
questions.why: Paint does not stick to oil, scale and spatter, and sharp edges and burrs are a hazard. In salt air bare steel rusts within days, so it is cleaned and primed promptly.

questions.q: A wired edge is to be made round a 3 mm wire. Using the usual rule, what allowance should be added?
o: About 3.0 mm
About 6.0 mm
About 7.5 mm
About 9.0 mm
questions.why: A common allowance for a wired edge is 2.5 times the wire diameter: 2.5 × 3 = 7.5 mm. Too little and the edge will not close round the wire.

questions.q: Shanelle is hollowing a copper dish in a sandbag. The metal has become springy and is starting to crack at the edge. What should she do?
o: Hammer harder to finish before it cracks further
Switch to a steel ball-pein hammer for more force
Cool it in water after every few blows
Anneal it, then carry on hollowing
questions.why: Hammering cold copper work hardens it until it cracks. Annealing (heating to a dull red, then cooling) softens it so hollowing can continue.

questions.q: Romaine marks each bend line on a long panel by measuring from the line before it. The bends come out unevenly spaced. What should he do?
o: Measure every line from one datum edge
Use a longer tape measure for the whole job
Mark the lines with a deeper scribe
Measure from the far end instead
questions.why: Measuring each line from the last one adds up small errors. Measuring every line from one datum keeps each error small and separate.
